          Has the WSL Become More Competitive Than Ever?
        
      
                          
                      Oct 13, 2026
          
                      Maya Shah / Author, Emily Millen / Design, Yash Thakur / Data Viz
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Five matchdays into the 2026-27 WSL season, the established hierarchy is under pressure as Arsenal struggle and Tottenham and London City Lionesses mount a push for Europe. But is the WSL genuinely more competitive than ever?
The 2026-27 Women’s Super League season is already challenging our pre-season expectations.
Arsenal are languishing in the bottom half, London City Lionesses and Tottenham are pushing for European qualification, and the traditional ‘big four' are facing competition from the chasing pack.

Results have been very unpredictable as well. Teams outside the usual elite are taking points off their more decorated opponents at a record rate, while the gap between the league's traditional powers and new challengers looks like it's shrinking. The three promoted sides are also showing signs of both promise and vulnerability in equal measure.
The only stable element seems to be reigning champions Manchester City, who have made a perfect start to their title defence.
So, with five matchdays played, is the WSL really becoming more competitive? We examine five key trends in the data to find out.

If there has been one recurring theme among WSL fans this season, it is that the league feels harder to call. There are fewer games that look straightforward on paper, particularly in the middle of the table where the gap between teams is becoming increasingly difficult to see.

Arsenal sitting 10th with five points after five games is the most obvious example. Manchester United, meanwhile, are three places above them in seventh. We're only five matchdays in, but the Red Devils have only finished above Arsenal once in WSL history, in 2022-23, when they finished second and Arsenal third.

Results to date have given us a lot of contrasting conclusions. London City opened their campaign by beating Man Utd, before losing to West Ham. United then beat West Ham, while Tottenham subsequently defeated the Hammers before being thumped 6-1 by London City. It definitely feels like anyone can beat anyone.

The data supports that theory as well.  Non-big four sides are averaging a record 0.42 points per game against the big four, the highest on record across a season since 2015 (0.43), while it is up from 0.30 last season.

There's something in the data that should give us pause here, though. At the moment, teams with a higher expected goals (xG) total have won just 62.9% of those matches, the lowest rate since Opta’s updated model was introduced in 2021-22. So there is a chance that the big four teams have just been on the receiving end of some unusual results in the opening stages of the campaign.

Underperformance against expected goals is something that's afflicting the league as a whole this season. The league-wide difference between goals scored and xG stands at -3.88, the first time it's been a negative figure in a WSL season since Opta's xG model was recently updated.
What’s even more interesting is that sides outside the traditional big four have been responsible for some of the biggest wins in the WSL season so far.

London City (6-1 vs Tottenham), Brighton (5-1 vs Charlton), Liverpool (4-0 vs Charlton) and Tottenham (7-0 vs Crystal Palace; 4-0 vs Aston Villa) have already produced five wins by a margin of four or more goals.

It is only the second time in WSL history that teams outside the traditional top four have recorded at least five such victories in a season. The only previous occasion was 2020-21, when there were eight; last season, there were just two.
By comparison, Chelsea are the only traditional big four side to have won by four or more goals this season, beating Man Utd 5-0 on MD2.

The established hierarchy is becoming less reliable, with more teams capable of producing convincing results against stronger opposition. That is perhaps the clearest evidence yet that the WSL is becoming more competitive.

The battle to break into the UWCL looks considerably more possible than it did for the chasing pack at the start of the season, as both London City Lionesses and Tottenham have made impressive starts.

Spurs have scored 16 goals, the joint-most in the WSL alongside Man City, with London City side just behind on 15. Tottenham’s attacking threat was particularly clear in their 7-0 win over Crystal Palace, when all seven goals came in the second half – the first time in WSL history a team had scored seven goals after half-time.
While London City’s aggressive squad overhaul initially sparked debate over whether a group of superstars could fit together immediately, the team is quickly proving they can.
